title: Katha, Chandogya and Isha: "That Art Thou"
bigQuestion: How do the Upanishads use questions, teachers and simple images to teach about the self and Brahman?

story.title: Inside the Seed
story.kicker: A father hands his son a fig from a great tree and tells him to break it open.
paragraphs: Shvetaketu has come home after twelve years of study. He is twenty-four, and he is proud of how much he has learned. His father, Uddalaka Aruni, asks him a question he cannot answer. Did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, and the unknown becomes known?

Over many days, the father teaches with things close at hand. One day he says: bring me a fruit from that banyan tree. Shvetaketu brings it. Break it, says his father. What do you see? Tiny seeds, sir. Break one of them. What do you see? Nothing at all, sir.

The father says that from this fine essence, which you cannot see, this great banyan tree stands. Then he says the words that close each lesson in this part of the Chandogya Upanishad. That fine essence is the self of all this. That is the real. That is the self. That art thou, Shvetaketu.

The Sanskrit is *tat tvam asi*. Hindu teachers have discussed those three words for well over a thousand years. Some read them as saying the self and Brahman are one. Others read them as saying the self depends on Brahman as a body depends on its soul. The debate is still alive.

In this chapter you will read three Upanishads closely: the Katha, where a boy questions Death himself, the Chandogya, and the short Isha. You will practice reading a dialogue: who asks, who answers, and what image carries the idea.
story.think: The father could have simply told his son the answer. Why might he have asked him to break open the seed instead?

lessons.title: Texts at the End of the Veda
lessons.mainIdea: The Upanishads are the last layer of the Vedas, and many Hindus call them Vedanta, the end of the Veda.
reading: The *Upanishads* are Sanskrit texts that form the last layer of the Vedas. The earlier layers are the hymns, the ritual manuals and the forest texts. The Upanishads turn from ritual to questions about the self, the world and what is ultimately real. For this reason tradition calls them *Vedanta*, the end or goal of the Veda.

Hindu tradition counts more than a hundred Upanishads, but about thirteen are called the principal or early ones. They include the Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya, Katha, Isha and Mundaka. Scholars usually date the oldest, the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya, to about the 7th or 6th century BCE, and others such as the Katha to later centuries BCE.

Hindus who follow the Vedas regard the Upanishads as *shruti*, "what was heard": revealed texts, not composed by human authors in the ordinary sense. Scholars describe how the texts were composed and passed down orally in different schools of Vedic priests. Both views are part of the story students should know.

words.d: Sanskrit texts forming the last layer of the Vedas, focused on the self and ultimate reality
"end of the Veda"; the Upanishads, and the schools of thought based on them
"what was heard"; texts many Hindus regard as revealed, including the Vedas and Upanishads

look.title: Four Layers of Each Veda
look.cite: Standard scholarly outline of the Vedic corpus, e.g. Patrick Olivelle, Upanisads (Oxford, 1996), introduction (summarized)
look.prompt: Why would the layer that asks the deepest questions come last? What might have changed over time?

check.q: Why are the Upanishads called Vedanta?
choices: They are the end or goal of the Veda
They are the first hymns of the Rig Veda
They are part of the Mahabharata
check.why: Vedanta means end of the Veda; the Upanishads are the last Vedic layer.

check.q: Which two Upanishads do scholars usually count as the oldest?
check.why: Scholars place Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya earliest, c. 7th–6th century BCE.

check.q: What does shruti mean?
choices: What was heard; texts many Hindus regard as revealed
check.why: Shruti means heard; smriti means remembered.

lessons.title: How to Read a Dialogue
lessons.mainIdea: Upanishads often teach through dialogues, so readers ask who asks, who answers, and what image carries the idea.
reading: Many Upanishads are not lectures. They are conversations. A son asks his father. A wife asks her husband. A boy asks the god of death. A student sits near a teacher. The word upanishad is often explained as "sitting down near," though scholars debate the exact meaning.

When you read a *dialogue*, ask three questions. First, who asks and who answers? The asker's situation shapes the teaching. Second, what does the teacher do: tell, show, test or tell a story? Third, what *image* carries the idea: salt, a seed, a chariot, a river?

These questions help because the Upanishads rarely give a definition and stop. They show an idea working in a scene. A careful reader follows the scene, writes down the image, and then asks what the teacher wants the student to see. You will use these three questions all through this chapter.

words.d: a teaching carried out as a conversation between speakers
a concrete picture, like salt or a seed, that carries an abstract idea
the basic pair in Upanishadic teaching; the student asks, the teacher shows

look.title: Three Questions for Any Dialogue
look.text: 1. Who asks and who answers? 2. What does the teacher do: tell, show, test or tell a story? 3. What image carries the idea? Try them on this: A father tells his son to put salt in water overnight and bring it in the morning.
look.prompt: Answer the three questions for the salt scene, even before you read it in full. What do you predict the teacher wants to show?

check.q: What is the common explanation of the word upanishad?
check.why: Upanishad is often explained as sitting down near, though scholars debate it.

check.q: Which is one of the three questions for reading a dialogue?
check.why: Asking what image carries the idea is a reading tool; judging truth is not our task.

check.q: Why do readers watch the scene rather than look for a definition?
choices: The Upanishads often show ideas in scenes instead of defining them
The scenes are always about war
check.why: The texts teach through scenes and images.

lessons.title: A Boy at Death's Door
lessons.mainIdea: In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa goes to Yama, the lord of death, and is granted three wishes.
reading: The Katha Upanishad opens with a sacrifice. A man named Vajashravasa is giving away his possessions, but the cows he gives are old and dry. His young son Nachiketa is troubled and asks, "To whom will you give me?" He asks a second and third time. At last his angry father says, "To Death I give you."

Nachiketa goes to the house of *Yama*, the lord of death, who is away. The boy waits three nights without food. When Yama returns, he feels he has wronged a guest, and offers three wishes, one for each night. This is how the Upanishad sets up its teaching.

Nachiketa's first wish is that his father be calm and welcome him home. His second is to learn a fire ritual that leads to heaven. His third is the great question: when a person dies, some say he exists and some say he does not. I want to know this. The rest of the Upanishad is Yama's answer.

words.d: the lord of death in Hindu texts, and Nachiketa's teacher in the Katha Upanishad
the boy who questions Yama in the Katha Upanishad
a wish granted as a gift; Yama grants Nachiketa three

look.title: Three Wishes
look.text: Katha Upanishad 1.1 (summary): Wish 1: that his father be at peace and welcome him back. Wish 2: to learn the fire ritual that leads to heaven. Wish 3: to know what happens to a person after death.
look.prompt: How do the wishes move from near to far? Why might the Upanishad save the deepest question for last?

check.q: Why does Nachiketa go to Yama?
choices: His angry father says, "To Death I give you"
He is lost in the forest
check.why: In Katha 1.1 his father, angered by his questions, gives him to Death.

check.q: Why does Yama grant three wishes?
choices: The boy defeated him in debate
The boy waited three nights without food as a guest
check.why: Yama makes up for three nights of an unwelcomed guest.

check.q: What is Nachiketa's third wish?
choices: To know what happens to a person after death
check.why: The third wish asks about existence after death.

lessons.title: The Good and the Pleasant
lessons.mainIdea: Yama tests Nachiketa with riches, and praises him for choosing the good over the pleasant.
reading: Yama does not answer at once. He says even the gods had doubts about this question, and he asks Nachiketa to choose another wish. He offers sons and grandsons, cattle, horses, gold, a long life and a great kingdom, even lovely companions with chariots and music.

Nachiketa refuses. These things last only until tomorrow, he says, and they wear out the senses. Wealth cannot make a person content. Keep your horses and your songs. The wish I choose is the one I asked. Yama is pleased. He has tested the student and found him ready.

In Katha 1.2 Yama teaches that there are two things, the good, *shreyas*, and the pleasant, *preyas*. Both bind a person to action. The wise choose the good; the foolish choose the pleasant for the sake of comfort. Many Hindu teachers use this pair when they speak about choices young people face.

words.d: the good: what truly benefits a person, in the Katha Upanishad
the pleasant: what gives quick pleasure
a trial by a teacher to see if a student is ready

look.title: Good or Pleasant?
look.text: Katha 1.2.1–2 (paraphrase): The good is one thing, the pleasant another. The wise one weighs them and chooses the good over the pleasant; the foolish one chooses the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.
look.prompt: Describe a choice a student might face between the good and the pleasant. Why does Yama test Nachiketa before teaching him?

check.q: What does Yama offer Nachiketa instead of an answer?
choices: Wealth, long life, a kingdom and pleasures
A place in the Pandava army
check.why: In Katha 1.1 Yama offers many riches to turn Nachiketa aside.

check.q: What is shreyas?
choices: The pleasant, what feels good now
check.why: Shreyas is the good; preyas is the pleasant.

check.q: Why is Yama pleased with Nachiketa?
choices: He chose the good over riches
check.why: By refusing riches, Nachiketa shows he is ready to learn.

lessons.title: The Chariot
lessons.mainIdea: Katha Upanishad 1.3.3 to 1.3.4 pictures the self as the rider in a chariot drawn by the senses.
reading: One of the most famous images in the Upanishads comes in Katha 1.3. Yama says: know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot. The intellect, *buddhi*, is the charioteer, and the mind is the reins. The senses are the horses, and the objects of the senses are the roads they run on.

Yama explains what the image means. A person without understanding, whose mind is never held firm, has senses like wild horses that do not obey the driver. A person with understanding, whose mind is held firm, has senses like good horses. Such a person reaches the end of the road.

Students may notice that the Gita also uses a chariot, with Krishna as Arjuna's driver. Scholars often compare the two images. The Katha's chariot is inside every person. Readers across Hindu schools use it to talk about self-control, and it is often drawn in Hindu children's books.

words.d: the intellect or understanding; the charioteer in the Katha image
Katha 1.3.3–4: self as rider, body as chariot, intellect as driver, mind as reins, senses as horses
the ability to steer one's actions; the Katha pictures it as a driver with firm reins

look.title: The Rider in the Chariot
look.text: Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins.
look.cite: Katha Upanishad 1.3.3, tr. F. Max Müller, The Upanishads, part 2 (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884)
look.prompt: Match each part of the chariot to a part of the person. Which part does the steering, and which part only rides?

check.q: In the Katha chariot image, what are the horses?
check.why: Katha 1.3.4 calls the senses the horses.

check.q: Who is the charioteer in Katha 1.3.3?
check.why: The intellect drives; the mind is the reins; the self is the rider.

check.q: How does the Katha chariot differ from the Gita's chariot?
choices: The Katha's is drawn by elephants
The Katha's is an image inside every person; the Gita's is part of the story
check.why: The Gita's chariot carries Arjuna; the Katha's is a picture of the self.

lessons.title: That Art Thou
lessons.mainIdea: In Chandogya Upanishad 6, Uddalaka teaches his son that the finest essence is the self of all, ending: tat tvam asi.
reading: Chandogya Upanishad chapter 6 is a series of lessons from Uddalaka Aruni to his son Shvetaketu. Each lesson uses an everyday example: clay and pots, bees and honey, rivers and the sea. Each one ends with the same words. This refrain appears nine times, from 6.8.7 to 6.16.3.

The refrain says that the finest essence is the self of all that exists. It is the real. It is the self. That art thou, Shvetaketu. In Sanskrit the last phrase is *tat tvam asi*. Tradition counts it as one of the four *mahavakyas*, the great sayings of the Upanishads.

What does it mean? Teachers of Advaita Vedanta read it as saying the self, atman, is identical with *Brahman*, ultimate reality. Teachers of other Vedanta schools read it as saying the self belongs to Brahman and depends on it, but is not the same. You will study these readings in depth in unit 15.

words.d: "That art thou"; the refrain of Chandogya Upanishad 6
"great saying"; four short Upanishad sayings tradition treats as summing up their teaching
in the Upanishads, the ultimate reality behind all things

look.title: The Refrain
look.text: It is the True. It is the Self, and thou, O Svetaketu, art it.
look.cite: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7, tr. F. Max Müller, The Upanishads, part 1 (Sacred Books of the East 1, 1879)
look.prompt: Who speaks, and to whom? What does "it" refer to? Why might a teacher repeat this line at the end of each lesson?

check.q: Who teaches Shvetaketu in Chandogya 6?
check.why: Uddalaka teaches his son in Chandogya 6; Yama teaches in the Katha.

check.q: What is a mahavakya?
choices: A great saying of the Upanishads
check.why: Tat tvam asi is one of four mahavakyas.

check.q: How does Advaita Vedanta read tat tvam asi?
choices: The self is wholly separate from Brahman
The self is identical with Brahman
It is a greeting between friends
check.why: Advaita reads the saying as identity of atman and Brahman; other schools read it differently.

lessons.title: The Banyan Seed
lessons.mainIdea: In Chandogya 6.12, a seed broken open shows nothing visible, yet from that fine essence a great tree grows.
reading: In Chandogya 6.12, Uddalaka asks for a fruit of the nyagrodha, the banyan tree. He has his son break it and asks what he sees. Tiny seeds, the son says. Break one. What do you see? Nothing at all, sir. The seed's inner core is too fine to see. The scene is short, but every step matters.

The father answers that from this fine essence which you do not see, this great banyan stands. Believe it, my dear, he says. Then comes the refrain: that fine essence is the self of all; that art thou. The lesson moves from the visible tree to the invisible source.

The banyan is a fitting choice. It is a huge tree whose branches send down roots, so one tree can look like a forest. The image teaches that something great can come from something too small to see. Readers note how the teacher lets the student discover the "nothing" himself before naming it.

words.d: the banyan tree; its fruit is broken open in Chandogya 6.12
the finest inner nature of something; Chandogya 6 calls it the self of all
not able to be seen; the seed's core, and the essence it stands for

look.title: Break It
look.text: Bring a fruit of that banyan tree. Break it. What do you see? These tiny seeds, sir. Break one of them. What do you see? Nothing at all, sir.
look.cite: Chandogya Upanishad 6.12.1, paraphrased from F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 1, 1879)
look.prompt: Count the steps in this dialogue. Why does the teacher ask the student to break the seed himself?

check.q: What does Shvetaketu see when he breaks a seed?
check.why: In Chandogya 6.12 the seed's core is too fine to see.

check.q: What does the banyan lesson teach, according to the father?
choices: Trees are more important than people
Banyans are sacred only in Chicago
From an unseen fine essence the great tree grows
check.why: The visible tree comes from an invisible essence.

check.q: What teaching method does the father use?
choices: He lets the student discover by doing
He sends the student to Yama
check.why: The student breaks the seed and sees for himself.

lessons.title: Salt in Water
lessons.mainIdea: In Chandogya 6.13, salt dissolved in water cannot be seen but can be tasted everywhere in it.
reading: In the next lesson, Chandogya 6.13, Uddalaka tells his son to put a lump of salt in water and come back in the morning. In the morning he says: bring me the salt you put in the water. The son looks, but cannot find it, because it has dissolved. The lump seems simply gone.

Taste the water from the top, the father says. How is it? Salty. Taste from the middle. Salty. Taste from the bottom. Salty. The salt is everywhere in the water, though you cannot see it. So too, the father says, you do not see the real here, but it is here.

The image adds something the seed did not. The seed showed something too small to see. The salt shows something present everywhere at once, known by taste rather than sight. Many teachers use the salt lesson to explain how the Upanishads picture Brahman as present in all things.

words.d: to mix into a liquid until it can no longer be seen
to be present in every part of something
sat; Chandogya 6's word for the being that underlies all things

look.title: Seed and Salt Side by Side
look.text: Chandogya 6.12: a seed is broken, and its core is too fine to see, yet a banyan grows from it. Chandogya 6.13: salt vanishes in water, yet every sip tastes of it.
look.prompt: What does each image teach that the other does not? Why might a teacher use both?

check.q: Why can Shvetaketu not find the salt?
choices: It has dissolved in the water
check.why: The salt dissolved overnight.

check.q: How does he know the salt is still there?
choices: He sees it at the bottom
His father tells him without testing
check.why: Tasting from top, middle and bottom shows it is present throughout.

check.q: What does the salt lesson add to the seed lesson?
choices: The essence can be seen with care
The essence belongs only to trees
The essence is present everywhere at once
check.why: The salt pervades all the water, known by taste, not sight.

lessons.title: Enjoy by Renouncing
lessons.mainIdea: Isha Upanishad 1 says all this world is pervaded by the Lord, and one should enjoy by renouncing and not covet.
reading: The Isha Upanishad is very short, only eighteen verses. It is found as the last chapter of the Vajasaneyi Samhita of the White Yajur Veda. It takes its name from its first word, isha, "the Lord." Many Hindus know its opening verse by heart. It is often chanted at the start of study.

Isha 1 says that all this, whatever moves in the moving world, is to be covered or pervaded by the Lord. Then it gives advice: enjoy through renouncing, and do not covet anyone's wealth. The Sanskrit phrase tena tyaktena bhunjitha, "enjoy by what has been given up," puzzles and delights readers.

How can a person enjoy by *renouncing*? One reading: if the world belongs to the Lord, a person can use and enjoy things without grasping them as "mine." Gandhi said that if all the Upanishads were lost and only this verse remained, Hinduism would live on. He read it as a call to simple living and trusteeship.

words.d: "the Lord"; the first word and name of the Isha Upanishad
to give up or let go of; Isha 1 says to enjoy by renouncing
to want what belongs to someone else; Isha 1 says do not covet

look.title: The Opening Verse
look.text: All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is pervaded by the Lord. Enjoy it by letting go; do not covet anyone's wealth.
look.cite: Isha Upanishad 1, paraphrased from F. Max Müller, The Upanishads, part 1 (Sacred Books of the East 1, 1879)
look.prompt: How can someone enjoy something by letting go of it? Give one example from ordinary life.

check.q: Where is the Isha Upanishad found?
choices: As the last chapter of the Vajasaneyi Samhita of the White Yajur Veda
In Book 10 of the Rig Veda
check.why: The Isha is chapter 40 of the Vajasaneyi Samhita.

check.q: What does Isha 1 tell a person not to do?
check.why: Isha 1 ends: do not covet anyone's wealth.

check.q: What did Gandhi say about Isha 1?
choices: It should be removed from the Vedas
If only this verse survived, Hinduism would live on
It is about the dice game
check.why: Gandhi praised the verse as containing the heart of Hinduism.

lessons.title: Seeing All in the Self
lessons.mainIdea: Isha 6 and 7 say that one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, feels no hatred or grief.
reading: Isha verses 6 and 7 turn from the world to the one who sees it. A person who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, does not shrink away from anything, or, as some translate, feels no hatred. When all beings have become one's own self, what delusion or grief can there be for the one who sees that oneness?

These verses link the Upanishad's big idea to how a person treats others. If the self is in all beings, then harming another is like harming oneself. Many Hindu teachers, and some Jain and Buddhist writers with their own reasons, connect this kind of seeing to compassion.

The Gita has a close parallel in 6.29, which describes the yogi who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Readers compare such passages across texts, a practice called intertextual reading. It shows how ideas travel from the Upanishads into the Gita.

words.d: the state of being one; Isha 7 speaks of seeing all beings as one's own self
a passage in another text that says something similar
reading one text beside another to see how ideas connect

look.title: Isha 6 and Gita 6.29
look.text: Isha 6 (paraphrase): one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, feels no hatred. Gita 6.29 (paraphrase): the yogi sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, and sees the same everywhere.
look.prompt: What words are nearly the same? What is different about the setting of each passage?

check.q: What does Isha 6 say about one who sees the self in all beings?
check.why: Isha 6 links this seeing with freedom from hatred or shrinking away.

check.q: Which Gita verse closely parallels Isha 6?
check.why: Gita 6.29 describes seeing the self in all beings and all beings in the self.

check.q: What is intertextual reading?
choices: Reading one text beside another to see connections
check.why: Intertextual reading compares passages across texts.
